data.title: Meridian Pavilion
data.shortDescription: Six vaulted halls that frame the Zayandeh River at dawn.

hero.alt: Six vaulted halls of the Meridian Pavilion reflected in a still pool at dawn

description: The Meridian Pavilion lines up six vaulted halls along the line of the old Isfahan meridian, so that each hall opens to the river at a slightly different angle of morning light.
The halls are cast in lime-pigmented concrete and share a single shallow pool, which doubles the arcade in water and cools the air before it enters the building.

panels.heading: A hall for every hour
body: Each vault is oriented a few degrees from its neighbour. As the sun climbs, the glow moves from the first hall to the last, turning the pavilion into a slow instrument for telling time.
Programme: a 600-seat hall, three exhibition rooms, a reading garden and a café at the river edge.

image.alt: The arcade seen from the pool edge

panels.caption: The arcade from the pool edge, late morning.

panels.text: “We wanted the building to arrive slowly, the way light arrives at a courtyard.”

image.alt: Interior of the main hall with three arched openings

panels.caption: Main hall: three arched openings frame the river.

panels.heading: Site
panels.body: The plot sits 300 m north-west of Si-o-se-pol, where the river widens. Foot traffic from the old bridge enters at the third hall.

images.alt: Terracotta fins of the south facade

captions: South facade: terracotta fins, 40 mm apart.

panels.caption: Longitudinal section: the roofs step down toward the river.

data.title: Tehran Terraces
data.shortDescription: Sixty homes stacked as planted terraces facing the Alborz.

hero.alt: Tehran Terraces, six stepped levels planted with trees against the Alborz foothills

description: Tehran Terraces turns a steep north-facing plot into sixty apartments, each with a private garden terrace as large as its living room.
The stepped section lets every home look over the roof of the one below, and keeps the street edge at the scale of the neighbouring houses.

body: Every terrace is a garden: planters are cast into the slab edge, irrigated from the building’s grey-water system.
From the street the building reads as a hill; from the terraces it reads as a village.

image.alt: Garden terraces in a wide view

panels.caption: Planted terraces catch the afternoon light.

panels.text: “The terrace is the room we never had in the apartment block.”

panels.caption: Screens of thermally modified ash, 12 mm slats.

image.alt: Living room opening onto the terrace

panels.caption: A living room opens onto its own garden.
Section A-A: each level is set back 3.6 m.

panels.heading: Neighbourhood
panels.body: The site is on the slopes of Darabad, 1,650 m above sea level. Views run north to Mount Tochal.

data.title: Caspian Reading House
data.shortDescription: A public library arranged around a rain-fed water court.

hero.alt: Aerial view of the Caspian Reading House ringed around a water court

description: The Reading House is a ring of twelve small pavilions around a rain-fed water court. Each pavilion holds one reading room with a single large window to the court.
Rasht’s wet climate becomes the building’s main material: rainwater is collected, slowed and displayed rather than hidden.

body: Twelve pavilions, twelve atmospheres. Each reading room has its own ceiling height, its own timber and its own view of the water.
The ring is open on the south, where the garden meets the city street.

image.alt: The water court seen from above

panels.caption: The water court, seen from the roof garden.

image.alt: A reading room with arched windows

panels.caption: Reading room 07: arched windows, oak joinery.

panels.text: “A library should feel like shelter in the rain, not like storage.”

panels.caption: The timber screen filters the low Caspian sun.
First floor plan, 1:200 — twelve pavilions around the court.

data.title: Zagros Lodge
data.shortDescription: Stone volumes set into a mountain valley like boulders.

hero.alt: Zagros Lodge: stone volumes catching low sun in the mountains

description: Zagros Lodge is a cluster of eight stone volumes that follow the fall of the valley. The rooms are small, deep and warm; the shared spaces are large and open to the mountains.
All stone comes from a quarry four kilometres away, and the lodge runs on a micro-hydro turbine in the stream below.

body: The lodge is arranged in a loose line so that every room sees the valley and none sees another room.
Walls are 60 cm thick, giving the rooms a calm thermal inertia through the long mountain winter.

panels.caption: The valley at golden hour.
Dry-laid stone, 60 cm wall section.

panels.text: “You sleep inside the mountain, and wake up inside the view.”

image.alt: A suite interior with arched openings

panels.caption: Suite 12: three arched openings frame the ridge.

panels.heading: Valley
panels.body: Chelgerd sits at 2,300 m. Winter snow lies for five months; the lodge opens year-round with a ski-in route from the north ridge.

panels.caption: Site plan, 1:1000 — eight volumes on the contour.

data.title: Hormuz Shore Walk
data.shortDescription: A kilometre-long timber promenade lifted above the tide.

hero.alt: The Hormuz Shore Walk, a long timber promenade raised above the water

description: The Shore Walk raises a one-kilometre promenade above the tidal flats on slender piers, giving the city a new horizon line to walk along.
Under the walk, the mangrove nursery is restored; above it, shaded pavilions, benches and a fish market face the Strait.

body: The walk follows the old shoreline, which the city had forgotten. Where the tide once reached, there are now benches; where fishermen landed, a market.
It is built in 24 prefabricated bays, each lifted into place in a single tide.

panels.caption: The promenade at mid-tide.

panels.text: “For the first time the city faces the water with its front, not its back.”

panels.caption: At dusk the walk fills with families.
Slatted deck: 18 mm gaps drain the spray.
Promenade plan, 1:1000.

panels.heading: The Strait
panels.body: Bandar Abbas faces the Strait of Hormuz; the tidal range here is 3.4 m. The piers are designed for 50-year storm surge.

data.title: Green Spine Masterplan
data.shortDescription: A 120-hectare district stitched together by one continuous park.

hero.alt: Aerial masterplan of the Green Spine, courtyards arranged around a central basin

description: The masterplan organises 120 hectares of former industrial land along a single continuous park, the Green Spine, with courtyards of mixed use set on either side.
Every home is within a five-minute walk of the spine, and the spine itself is a flood channel, a cycle route and a public garden.

panels.heading: One park, many courtyards
body: The Green Spine is where the district drains, walks and gathers. Courtyard blocks give it edges; shops and schools give it reasons to be crossed.
The plan is phased in four stages of eight years each, and is designed to be useful at every stage.

panels.caption: Masterplan, 1:5000.

image.alt: Aerial view of a district block

panels.caption: A typical courtyard block, 80 × 80 m.

panels.text: “A district is not a plan; it is the sum of how people cross it.”

panels.caption: Typical street: 18 m wide, trees on both sides.
Street section, 1:100.

data.title: Naqsh Atelier Interior
data.shortDescription: A gallery and workshop carved from a former printing house.

hero.alt: Three arched openings glowing in the Naqsh Atelier gallery

description: The atelier turns a former printing house into a gallery, a workshop and a library. Arched openings cut into the old brick walls borrow light from the courtyard.
Furniture is built from the demolished interior — every bench and table has a former life as a floor joist or a print-room shelf.

body: The existing brick walls were left raw. New work is limited to three gestures: the arched openings, a timber floor and a ceiling of warm light.
In the evening the arches glow like lanterns from the street.

panels.caption: The gallery: five openings, one axis.

panels.text: “Nothing here was bought new. Everything is the building remembering itself.”

panels.caption: A timber screen divides workshop and gallery.
The courtyard arcade, added in the second phase.
Floor plan, 1:50.

panels.heading: Address
panels.body: Enghelab Street, near the bookshop quarter. The atelier is open Saturday to Wednesday, 09:00–17:00.

data.title: Kavir Observatory
data.shortDescription: A research dome and a low visitor wing in the dark desert sky.

hero.alt: The Kavir Observatory dome above the desert dunes

description: The Kavir Observatory sits at the edge of a protected dark-sky zone. A research dome on a stout drum rises from the dunes; a low visitor wing hides behind them.
All lighting is below the horizon line, and the building is clad in the colour of the desert so that it disappears by day.

body: By day the observatory is a quiet silhouette on the dunes. By night the dome opens and the visitors’ wing glows at the horizon line, no higher.
The drum is cast on site with local sand and lime, giving it the colour and temperature of the ground.

panels.caption: At night the dome opens to the sky.

panels.text: “The darkest thing we built here is the lighting plan.”

panels.caption: The researchers’ tower, five stacked volumes.
Visitor terraces cut into the dune.
Section through the dome, 1:100.

panels.heading: Desert
panels.body: Garmsar is 120 km south-east of Tehran. The site is reached by a 9 km gravel road from the Kavir highway.
